notes.front: For Form 1041, who is a fiduciary?
notes.back: A trustee of a trust, or an executor, administrator, personal representative or person in possession of a decedent’s estate property.
notes.explanation: The definition covers both trusts (trustees) and estates (executors, administrators and similar representatives).
notes.example: Like a caretaker who holds someone else’s house keys: a trustee or executor manages property for the benefit of others.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Definitions: Fiduciary”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: A fiduciary is a trustee of a trust, or an executor, executrix, administrator, administratrix, personal representative, or person in possession of property of a decedent's estate.

notes.front: What three conditions make a trust a simple trust?
notes.back: Its instrument requires all income to be distributed currently; it provides nothing for charity; and it distributes no corpus.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must be met; a trust that fails any one of them is a complex trust.
notes.example: Like a pipe: everything that flows in as income flows straight out to the beneficiaries, and the principal stays put.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Simple Trust”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A trust may qualify as a simple trust if: 1. The trust instrument requires that all income must be distributed currently; 2. The trust instrument doesn't provide that any amounts are to be paid, permanently set aside, or used for charitable purposes; and 3. The trust doesn't distribute amounts allocated to the corpus of the trust.

notes.front: What is a complex trust?
notes.back: Any trust that does not qualify as a simple trust.
notes.explanation: The Form 1041 instructions define it purely by exclusion from the simple trust tests.
notes.example: Like a reservoir rather than a pipe: the trustee may hold income back, give to charity or pay out principal.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Complex Trust”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: Complex Trust A complex trust is any trust that doesn't qualify as a simple trust as explained above.

notes.front: What is a grantor type trust for income tax?
notes.back: A trust valid under state law that is not a separate taxable entity, because the grantor or other substantial owners have kept dominion and control.
notes.explanation: Because the owners have not given up complete dominion and control, the trust’s income is not taxed to the trust as a separate entity.
notes.example: Like putting savings in a box with your name on it that you can still open at will: the tax still follows you.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Grantor Type Trust”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: A grantor type trust is a legal trust under applicable state law that isn't recognized as a separate taxable entity for income tax purposes because the grantor or other substantial owners have not relinquished complete dominion and control over the trust.

notes.front: What is a qualified revocable trust?
notes.back: A trust treated as owned by the decedent on the day of death because the decedent held the power to revoke it.
notes.explanation: The instructions tie the status to the section 676 power to revoke held at death; a qualified revocable trust with a section 645 election is an electing trust.
notes.example: Like a living trust your aunt could have cancelled right up to her death: at death it becomes a qualified revocable trust.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Section 645 election: Qualified revocable trusts”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: In general, a QRT is any trust (or part of a trust) that, on the day the decedent died, was treated as owned by the decedent because the decedent held the power to revoke the trust as described in section 676. An electing trust is a QRT for which a section 645 election has been made.

notes.front: What is distributable net income (DNI) used for on Form 1041?
notes.back: It caps the income distribution deduction and sets how much of a distribution the beneficiary includes in gross income.
notes.explanation: The same figure, from Schedule B, line 7, drives both the trust’s deduction and the beneficiary’s inclusion.
notes.example: Like a ceiling on a lift: however much is distributed, no more than DNI is deducted by the trust or taxed to the beneficiary.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Distributable net income (DNI)”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The income distribution deduction allowable to estates and trusts for amounts paid, credited, or required to be distributed to beneficiaries is limited to DNI. This amount, which is figured on Schedule B, line 7, is also used to determine how much of an amount paid, credited, or required to be distributed to a beneficiary will be includible

notes.front: What is the accounting income of an estate or trust, and why must the fiduciary figure it first?
notes.back: Income under the will or trust instrument and local law; it fixes the income required to be distributed, on which the deduction partly rests.
notes.explanation: Tax rules do not define it: the governing instrument and local law do.
notes.example: Like a trust deed’s own rulebook for “income”: a dividend may count as income under it, but a gain on selling shares may not.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: the fiduciary must figure the accounting income of the estate or trust under the will or trust instrument and applicable local law to determine the amount, if any, of income that is required to be distributed, because the income distribution deduction is based, in part, on that amount.

notes.front: In trust accounting, what is corpus?
notes.back: The part of the trust allocated away from income under the governing instrument and local law; extraordinary dividends, for example, may belong to it.
notes.explanation: The instructions leave out of accounting income any extraordinary or taxable stock dividends that the instrument and local law allocate to corpus.
notes.example: Like the orchard as opposed to its apples: the trees stay in the trust, the fruit is income.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Schedule B, Line 8—Accounting Income”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Don't include extraordinary dividends or taxable stock dividends determined under the governing instrument and applicable local law to be allocable to corpus.

notes.front: What is the income distribution deduction of a trust or decedent’s estate?
notes.back: A deduction for distributions to beneficiaries, figured on Schedule B, which decides how much of the distributions is taxed to the beneficiaries.
notes.explanation: The instructions add that, for this reason, a trust or decedent’s estate is sometimes called a pass-through entity.
notes.example: Like handing on a bill: what the trust passes to beneficiaries it deducts, and they pay the tax instead.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A trust or decedent's estate is allowed an income distribution deduction for distributions to beneficiaries. To figure this deduction, the fiduciary must complete Schedule B. The income distribution deduction determines the amount of any distributions taxed to the beneficiaries. For this reason, a trust or decedent's estate is sometimes referred to as a "pass-through entity."

notes.front: What is a 501(c)(3) organization?
notes.back: An organisation exempt from federal income tax because it is organised and operated exclusively for purposes such as religious, charitable or scientific ones.
notes.explanation: Pub 557’s list of purposes continues beyond these four; the organisation must be organised and operated exclusively for them.
notes.example: Like a food bank or a church: set up and run only for a listed purpose, and exempt from income tax as a result.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Chapter 3. Section 501(c)(3) Organizations”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: An organization may qualify for exemption from federal income tax under section 501(c)(3) if it is organized and operated exclusively for one or more of the following purposes. • Religious. • Charitable. • Scientific. • Testing for public safety.

notes.front: What is a private foundation?
notes.back: Any 501(c)(3) organisation that does not fall into an excluded category, such as broadly supported public charities.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 makes private foundation the default: every 501(c)(3) organisation is one unless it is specifically excluded.
notes.example: Like a family’s charitable fund run from one endowment: it lacks broad public support, so it stays a private foundation.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Private Foundations”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: Every organization that qualifies for tax exemption as an organization described in section 501(c)(3) is a private foundation unless it falls into one of the categories specifically excluded from the definition of that term

notes.front: What is unrelated business taxable income (UBTI)?
notes.back: Gross income from any unrelated trade or business an exempt organisation regularly conducts, less the directly connected deductions.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 builds it from three ideas: a trade or business, regularly conducted, and unrelated to the exempt purpose.
notes.example: Like a wildlife charity running a commercial print shop for local firms: the shop’s profit, not the donations, is what gets taxed.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Chapter 4. Unrelated Business Taxable Income”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: The term "unrelated business taxable income" (UBTI) generally means the gross income derived from any unrelated trade or business regularly conducted by the exempt organization, less the deductions directly connected with carrying on the trade or business.

notes.front: How does a trust or decedent’s estate figure its gross income?
notes.back: In much the same way as an individual; most individual deductions and credits are also allowed.
notes.explanation: The major difference is the income distribution deduction for distributions to beneficiaries.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A trust or decedent's estate figures its gross income in much the same manner as an individual. Most deductions and credits allowed to individuals are also allowed to estates and trusts. However, there is one major distinction.

notes.front: A trust must distribute all its income currently, but its instrument also lets the trustee give $2,000 a year to a hospital charity. Simple or complex?
notes.back: Complex: a simple trust’s instrument must not provide for amounts to be paid, set aside or used for charity.
notes.choices:
A) Complex
B) Simple, because all income is distributed
C) Simple unless the gift is actually made
notes.choicesExplained: B: distributing all income is only one of three conditions. C: the test looks at what the instrument provides, not only what is paid.
notes.explanation: Condition 2 of the simple trust test is about the trust instrument: if it provides for charitable amounts, the trust is not simple.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Simple Trust”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: 2. The trust instrument doesn't provide that any amounts are to be paid, permanently set aside, or used for charitable purposes

notes.front: A trust must distribute all income currently and has no charitable terms. In 2025 the trustee also pays a beneficiary $15,000 of corpus. Simple or complex for 2025?
notes.back: Complex for 2025: a simple trust does not distribute amounts allocated to corpus.
notes.choices:
A) Complex for 2025
B) Simple, because its instrument meets the first two tests
C) It becomes a grantor trust
notes.choicesExplained: B: the third condition fails in a year corpus is distributed. C: paying out corpus says nothing about grantor control.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must hold; distributing $15,000 of corpus breaks the third one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Simple Trust”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: 3. The trust doesn't distribute amounts allocated to the corpus of the trust.

notes.front: A trust instrument lets the trustee decide each year whether to pay out income or add it to the fund. There are no charitable terms. Simple or complex?
notes.back: Complex: a simple trust’s instrument must require all income to be distributed currently.
notes.choices:
A) Complex
B) Simple, if the trustee happens to distribute all income
C) Simple, because there are no charitable terms
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test asks what the instrument requires, not what the trustee chooses. C: the lack of charitable terms is only one condition.
notes.explanation: Condition 1 needs a requirement in the trust instrument; a discretion to accumulate fails it.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Simple Trust”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The trust instrument requires that all income must be distributed currently

notes.front: If an entire trust is a grantor type trust (with no optional filing method), what goes on Form 1041?
notes.back: Only the entity information; dollar amounts go on an attachment, which must not be Schedule K-1.
notes.explanation: All figures go on an attachment rather than on the form or a Schedule K-1.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Grantor Type Trusts: How to report”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: If the entire trust is a grantor trust, fill in only the entity information of Form 1041. Don't show any dollar amounts on the form itself; show dollar amounts only on an attachment to the form. Don't use Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) as the attachment.

notes.front: During her life, Mei puts her investment portfolio into a revocable living trust she can change or end at any time. The trust earns $12,000 of dividends in 2025. Who is taxed on them?
notes.back: Mei: a revocable living trust is treated as a grantor type trust, so the income is not taxed to the trust as a separate entity.
notes.choices:
A) Mei, as grantor
B) The trust, at trust rates
C) Nobody until the trust ends
notes.choicesExplained: B: a grantor type trust is not a separate taxable entity. C: the income is taxed currently, to the grantor.
notes.explanation: Because she can revoke it, the trust is a grantor type trust for tax purposes.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Revocable living trust”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Because this type of trust is revocable, it is treated as a grantor type trust for tax purposes.

notes.front: For transfers in trust after 1 March 1986, when is a grantor treated as owner because of a reversionary interest?
notes.back: When, at the inception of that portion of the trust, the reversionary interest in income or corpus is worth more than 5% of that portion.
notes.explanation: The instructions measure the interest at inception against the value of the portion concerned.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Grantor Type Trust”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: the grantor is treated as the owner of any portion of a trust in which they have a reversionary interest in either the income or corpus therefrom, if, as of the inception of that portion of the trust, the value of the reversionary interest is more than 5% of the value of that portion.

notes.front: By when must Form 8855 be filed to make a section 645 election treating a qualified revocable trust as part of the estate?
notes.back: By the due date (including any extension granted) of Form 1041 for the related estate’s first tax year.
notes.explanation: The deadline applies even if the combined estate and trust have too little income to need a Form 1041.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Section 645 election”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: In general, Form 8855, Election To Treat a Qualified Revocable Trust as Part of an Estate, must be filed by the due date for Form 1041 for the first tax year of the related estate. This applies even if the combined related estate and electing trust don't have sufficient income to be required to file Form 1041.

notes.front: Once made, a section 645 election is {{c1::irrevocable}}.
notes.back: Irrevocable.
notes.explanation: The executor and trustee cannot later undo the choice to treat the qualified revocable trust as part of the estate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Section 645 election”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Once made, the election is irrevocable.

notes.front: Leo died on 10 March 2025 with a qualified revocable trust; no Form 706 is required and a section 645 election is made. Assets are not all distributed until 2028. When does the election period end?
notes.back: On 9 March 2027, the day before the applicable date of 10 March 2027 (2 years after death).
notes.choices:
A) 9 March 2027
B) When all assets are distributed in 2028
C) 31 December 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B: the period ends on the earlier of full distribution or the day before the applicable date. C: there is no calendar year-end rule.
notes.explanation: Step 1: no Form 706, so the applicable date is 2 years after death: 10 March 2027. Step 2: the day before is 9 March 2027, earlier than the 2028 distribution.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Election period”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: terminates on the earlier of: • The day on which the electing trust and related estate, if any, distribute all of their assets; or • The day before the applicable date.

notes.front: A trust meets the control test for domestic status if one or more U.S. persons have the authority to control {{c1::all substantial decisions}} of the trust.
notes.back: All substantial decisions.
notes.explanation: Control of only some substantial decisions is not enough: U.S. persons must control all of them.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Domestic and foreign trusts”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: One or more U.S. persons have the authority to control all substantial decisions of the trust (control test).

notes.front: A trust is supervised by a U.S. court, but a foreign person controls its substantial decisions. Which return does its trustee file?
notes.back: Form 1040-NR instead of Form 1041, because a trust that is not a domestic trust is a foreign trust.
notes.choices:
A) Form 1040-NR
B) Form 1041
C) No return at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 1041 is for domestic trusts; this one fails the control test. C: the trustee of a foreign trust files Form 1040-NR.
notes.explanation: Failing the control test makes it a foreign trust; one with a U.S. owner must generally also file Form 3520-A.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Domestic and foreign trusts”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: A trust that isn't a domestic trust is treated as a foreign trust. If you are the trustee of a foreign trust, file Form 1040-NR instead of Form 1041. Also, a foreign trust with a U.S. owner must generally file Form 3520-A

notes.front: How are abusive trust arrangements typically promoted?
notes.back: By promising tax benefits with no meaningful change in the taxpayer’s control over, or benefit from, their income or assets.
notes.explanation: The instructions say such arrangements claim to cut federal taxes in ways the law does not permit.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Abusive Trust Arrangements”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Certain trust arrangements claim to reduce or eliminate federal taxes in ways that are not permitted under the law. Abusive trust arrangements are typically promoted by the promise of tax benefits with no meaningful change in the taxpayer's control over or benefit from the taxpayer's income or assets.

notes.front: A promoter tells a client to put her home into a trust she still lives in and controls, then deduct depreciation on the home and her furnishings. What should you tell her?
notes.back: It bears the marks of an abusive trust arrangement: no real change in control, and depreciation on a personal residence is among the promised benefits.
notes.choices:
A) It is an abusive trust arrangement
B) It is a valid way to depreciate a home
C) It is valid if the trust gets its own employer identification number
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Form 1041 instructions list this depreciation among the benefits abusive trusts promise. C: an identification number does not change the lack of real change in control.
notes.explanation: The instructions name depreciation of an owner’s personal residence and furnishings among the benefits such arrangements promise.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Abusive Trust Arrangements”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: deductions for personal expenses paid by the trust; depreciation deductions of an owner's personal residence and furnishings; a stepped-up basis for property transferred to the trust;

notes.front: The {{c1::beneficiary}}, and not the trust or decedent’s estate, pays income tax on their distributive share of income.
notes.back: The beneficiary.
notes.explanation: Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) tells each beneficiary what to include on their own return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The beneficiary, and not the trust or decedent's estate, pays income tax on their distributive share of income. Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) is used to notify the beneficiaries of the amounts to be included on their income tax returns.

notes.front: A simple trust must distribute its accounting income of $25,000. Its distributable net income is $20,000, with no tax-exempt income. What is its income distribution deduction?
notes.back: $20,000: the deduction is limited to DNI, even though $25,000 is distributed.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the distribution is larger, but the deduction is capped at DNI. C: that is the excess over DNI, not the deduction.
notes.explanation: Step 1: amount required to be distributed = $25,000. Step 2: DNI = $20,000. Step 3: the deduction is the lower, $20,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Distributable net income (DNI)”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The income distribution deduction allowable to estates and trusts for amounts paid, credited, or required to be distributed to beneficiaries is limited to DNI.

notes.front: A trust has DNI of $18,000 and distributes $30,000 to its only beneficiary. How much of the $30,000 does DNI make includible in the beneficiary’s gross income?
notes.back: Up to $18,000: DNI also measures how much of a distribution the beneficiary includes.
notes.choicesExplained: B: amounts above DNI are not carried out as income by this rule. C: $12,000 is the excess of the distribution over DNI.
notes.explanation: Step 1: distribution $30,000. Step 2: DNI $18,000. The DNI figure caps what is includible: $18,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Distributable net income (DNI)”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: is also used to determine how much of an amount paid, credited, or required to be distributed to a beneficiary will be includible

notes.front: A complex trust receives $8,000 of ordinary dividends and a $50,000 extraordinary dividend that its instrument and local law allocate to corpus. What is its accounting income on Schedule B, line 8, from these items?
notes.back: $8,000: the extraordinary dividend allocated to corpus is left out.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the instructions exclude dividends allocable to corpus from accounting income. C: that is the corpus item, not income.
notes.explanation: Step 1: start with $8,000 + $50,000 = $58,000 received. Step 2: remove the $50,000 allocated to corpus, leaving $8,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Schedule B, Line 8—Accounting Income”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: If you are filing for a complex trust, enter the income for the tax year determined under the terms of the governing instrument and applicable local law. Don't include extraordinary dividends or taxable stock dividends determined under the governing instrument and applicable local law to be allocable to corpus.

notes.front: How do first-tier distributions differ from second-tier distributions on Schedule B?
notes.back: First-tier: income required to be distributed currently (line 9). Second-tier: other amounts, including distributions of corpus (line 10).
notes.explanation: Line 10 is completed only by a decedent’s estate or complex trust, and it also covers distributions of property in kind.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Schedule B, Line 10”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Line 10 is to be completed only by a decedent's estate or complex trust. These distributions consist of any other amounts paid, credited, or required to be distributed and are referred to as "second-tier distributions." Such amounts include annuities to the extent not paid out of income, mandatory and discretionary distributions of corpus, and distributions of property in kind.

notes.front: To what extent are first-tier distributions deductible by the trust and taxable to the beneficiary?
notes.back: Deductible to the extent of DNI; each beneficiary includes their proportionate share of DNI.
notes.explanation: Both the trust’s deduction and the beneficiary’s inclusion are measured against the same DNI.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Schedule B, Line 9”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: first-tier distributions" and are deductible by the estate or trust to the extent of the DNI. The beneficiary includes such amounts in their income to the extent of their proportionate share of the DNI.

notes.front: Who completes Schedule B, line 9 (income required to be distributed currently)?
notes.back: All simple trusts, and complex trusts and decedents’ estates required to distribute income currently, whether distributed or not.
notes.explanation: Whether income is required to be distributed depends on the governing instrument and local law.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Schedule B, Line 9”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: Line 9 is to be completed by all simple trusts as well as complex trusts and decedents' estates that are required to distribute income currently, whether it is distributed or not.

notes.front: A decedent’s estate is allowed an exemption of {{c1::$600}} on Form 1041.
notes.explanation: The exemption depends on the type of entity: estates, trusts that must distribute all income, and other trusts each have their own amount.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Decedents' estates. A decedent's estate is allowed a $600 exemption.

notes.front: A decedent’s estate has taxable income of $2,000 before its exemption. What exemption does it take, and what taxable income is left?
notes.back: A $600 exemption, leaving $1,400 of taxable income.
notes.choices:
A) $600, leaving $1,400
B) $300, leaving $1,700
C) $100, leaving $1,900
notes.choicesExplained: B: $300 is for trusts required to distribute all income currently. C: $100 is for other trusts.
notes.explanation: Step 1: a decedent’s estate gets $600. Step 2: $2,000 − $600 = $1,400.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Decedents' estates. A decedent's estate is allowed a $600 exemption.

notes.front: A trust whose governing instrument requires all income to be distributed currently is allowed a {{c1::$300}} exemption.
notes.explanation: The instructions tie this amount to the instrument’s requirement, not to what was actually distributed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: A trust whose governing instrument requires that all income be distributed currently is allowed a $300 exemption, even if it distributed amounts other than income during the tax year.

notes.front: A trust’s instrument requires all income to be distributed currently. In 2025 it also distributes $10,000 of corpus, so it is complex for the year. What exemption does it claim?
notes.back: $300: the exemption follows the instrument’s requirement, even if amounts other than income were distributed.
notes.choicesExplained: B: $100 is for trusts not required to distribute all income currently. C: $600 is the estate exemption.
notes.explanation: The instructions allow $300 to a trust required to distribute all income currently, even if it distributed amounts other than income that year.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: A trust whose governing instrument requires that all income be distributed currently is allowed a $300 exemption, even if it distributed amounts other than income during the tax year.

notes.front: A trust lets the trustee accumulate income at her discretion; it is not a qualified disability trust. What exemption does it claim on Form 1041?
notes.back: $100, the amount for all other trusts.
notes.choicesExplained: B: $300 needs an instrument requiring all income to be distributed currently. C: $600 is for decedents’ estates.
notes.explanation: A trust not described in the other categories is allowed a $100 exemption.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: All other trusts. A trust not described above is allowed a $100 exemption.

notes.front: A qualified disability trust is allowed a {{c1::$5,100}} exemption, which is not subject to phaseout.
notes.explanation: It is far larger than the $100 or $300 trust exemptions and is not reduced by a phaseout.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Line 21—Exemption”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Qualified disability trusts. A qualified disability trust is allowed a $5,100 exemption. This amount is not subject to phaseout.

notes.front: A domestic decedent’s estate must file Form 1041 if it has gross income for the tax year of {{c1::$600 or more}} (or a nonresident alien beneficiary).
notes.back: $600 or more.
notes.explanation: For an estate the test is gross income, not taxable income; a nonresident alien beneficiary triggers filing on its own.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Who Must File: Decedent’s Estate”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: The fiduciary (or one of the joint fiduciaries) must file Form 1041 for a domestic estate that has: 1. Gross income for the tax year of $600 or more; 2. A beneficiary who is a nonresident alien;

notes.front: A domestic trust with only U.S. beneficiaries has gross income of $450 and, after deductions and its exemption, taxable income of $40. Must it file Form 1041?
notes.back: Yes: a trust must file if it has any taxable income, even with gross income under $600.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because it has taxable income
B) No, because gross income is under $600
C) No, trusts file only with a nonresident alien beneficiary
notes.choicesExplained: B: $600 of gross income is only one of the triggers for a trust. C: a nonresident alien beneficiary is another trigger, not the only one.
notes.explanation: For trusts the list starts with any taxable income; $40 is enough, whatever the gross income.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Who Must File: Trust”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: must file Form 1041 for a domestic trust taxable under section 641 that has: 1. Any taxable income for the tax year; 2. Gross income of $600 or more (regardless of taxable income);

notes.front: A calendar-year estate or trust files its 2025 Form 1041 and Schedules K-1 by {{c1::15 April 2026}}.
notes.back: 15 April 2026.
notes.explanation: Fiscal-year estates and trusts instead use the 15th day of the 4th month after their year ends.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: For calendar year estates and trusts, file Form 1041 and Schedule(s) K-1 by April 15, 2026. For fiscal-year estates and trusts, file Form 1041 by the 15th day of the 4th month following the close of the tax year.

notes.front: An estate’s executor chose a fiscal year ending 31 January 2026. By when is that year’s Form 1041 due, and how long an extension can Form 7004 give?
notes.back: By 15 May 2026 (15th day of the 4th month after 31 January); Form 7004 gives an automatic 5½-month extension.
notes.choices:
A) 15 May 2026; 5½ months
B) 15 April 2026; 6 months
C) 30 April 2026; 5½ months
notes.choicesExplained: B: 15 April is the calendar-year date, and estates get 5½ months, not 6. C: the due date is the 15th day of the month, not month end.
notes.explanation: Step 1: count 4 months after January: February, March, April, May. Step 2: the 15th day gives 15 May 2026.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: For fiscal-year estates and trusts, file Form 1041 by the 15th day of the 4th month following the close of the tax year.

notes.front: An estate or trust uses Form 7004 to apply for an automatic {{c1::5½-month}} extension of time to file Form 1041.
notes.back: 5½-month.
notes.explanation: The request goes on Form 7004, the same application used for other business and information returns.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Extension of Time To File”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: use Form 7004, Application for Automatic Extension of Time To File Certain Business Income Tax, Information, and Other Returns, to apply for an automatic 51/2-month extension of time to file.

notes.front: Which of these may choose a fiscal year: a decedent’s estate, an ordinary non-grantor family trust, or both?
notes.back: Only the decedent’s estate; a trust generally must adopt a calendar year.
notes.choices:
A) Only the estate
B) Only the family trust
C) Both
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the family trust is not among the exempt trusts (tax-exempt, section 4947(a)(1) charitable, or wholly grantor-owned).
notes.explanation: Only the listed kinds of trust escape the calendar-year rule, and an ordinary family trust is not among them.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Accounting Periods”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Generally, a trust must adopt a calendar year. The following trusts are exempt from this requirement. • A trust that is exempt from tax under section 501(a). • A charitable trust described in section 4947(a)(1). • A trust that is treated as wholly owned by a grantor

notes.front: A calendar-year complex trust pays a beneficiary $6,000 on 20 February 2026. Can it treat the payment as made on 31 December 2025?
notes.back: Yes, by making the section 663(b) election: 20 February is day 51 after year end, within 65 days.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, with the section 663(b) election
B) No, payments after year end always fall in the next year
C) Yes, but only a decedent’s estate may elect
notes.choicesExplained: B: the election allows payments within 65 days to be treated as made on the last day of the year. C: a complex trust’s fiduciary may also elect.
notes.explanation: Step 1: January has 31 days; plus 20 days of February = day 51. Step 2: 51 ≤ 65, so the election is available.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Other Information, Question 6”, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: To make the section 663(b) election to treat any amount paid or credited to a beneficiary within 65 days following the close of the tax year as being paid or credited on the last day of that tax year, check the box. This election can be made by the fiduciary of a complex trust

notes.front: How does a trust elect under section 643(g) to pass estimated tax payments to beneficiaries, and by when?
notes.back: On Form 1041-T, filed by the 65th day after the tax year closes; the amount goes in box 13, code A, of the K-1.
notes.explanation: A decedent’s estate may make this election only for its final year.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: The fiduciary of a decedent's estate may make a section 643(g) election only for the final year of the estate. Make the election by filing Form 1041-T, Allocation of Estimated Tax Payments to Beneficiaries, by the 65th day after the close of the estate's or trust's tax year.

notes.front: A beneficiary disagrees with how the trust treated an item on her Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) and reports it differently. What must she do?
notes.back: File Form 8082 with her return to identify and explain the inconsistency.
notes.choices:
A) File Form 8082 with her return
B) Nothing: beneficiaries may report as they wish
C) Ask the trust to amend first; she cannot file otherwise
notes.choicesExplained: B: she must generally report items as the trust did. C: the instructions let her file with Form 8082 explaining the difference.
notes.explanation: The K-1 instructions require consistent treatment and a Form 8082 disclosure where the treatment differs.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) (2025), “Inconsistent Treatment of Items”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Generally, you must report items shown on your Schedule K-1 (including attached schedules) the same way that the estate or trust treated the items on its return. If the treatment of an item on your original or amended return is inconsistent with the estate's or trust's treatment

notes.front: When an estate or trust terminates, what character does each excess deduction passed to the beneficiary keep?
notes.back: Its own: an amount allowed in arriving at adjusted gross income, a non-miscellaneous itemized deduction, or a miscellaneous itemized deduction.
notes.explanation: Final regulations keep each excess deduction’s separate character when it passes to the beneficiary.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) (2025), “Reminders: Excess deductions on termination”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Under Final Regulations TD9918, each excess deduction on termination of an estate or trust retains its separate character as an amount allowed in arriving at adjusted gross income, a non-miscellaneous itemized deduction, or a miscellaneous itemized deduction.

notes.front: The late filing penalty on Form 1041 is 5% of the tax due for each month or part of a month, up to a maximum of {{c1::25%}} (unless the failure is fraudulent).
notes.explanation: A fraudulent failure raises the rate to 15% a month and the ceiling to 75%.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Late Filing of Return”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: The law provides a penalty of 5% of the tax due for each month, or part of a month, for which a return isn't filed up to a maximum of 25% of the tax due (15% for each month, or part of a month, up to a maximum of 75% if the failure to file is fraudulent).

notes.front: A trust files its Form 1041 70 days late, without reasonable cause and not fraudulently. The tax due is $300. What is the late filing penalty?
notes.back: $300. It is over 60 days late, so the minimum (smaller of $525 or the tax due) beats 5% × 3 months = $45.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the 60-day minimum overrides the monthly rate here. C: the minimum is the smaller of $525 or the tax due.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 70 days = 3 months or part months, 3 × 5% × $300 = $45. Step 2: minimum = smaller of $525 or $300 = $300. Step 3: the penalty is $300.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Late Filing of Return”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: If the return is more than 60 days late, the minimum penalty is the smaller of $525 or the tax due. The penalty won't be imposed if you can show that the failure to file on time was due to reasonable cause.

notes.front: What is the late payment penalty on tax shown on Form 1041?
notes.back: Generally ½ of 1% of the unpaid amount for each month or part month, up to 25%.
notes.explanation: The penalty is in addition to interest charged on late payments.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1041 (2025), “Late Payment of Tax”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Generally, the penalty for not paying tax when due is 1/2 of 1% of the unpaid amount for each month or part of a month it remains unpaid. The maximum penalty is 25% of the unpaid amount. The penalty applies to any unpaid tax on the return. Any penalty is in addition to interest charges on late payments.

notes.front: Are contributions to domestic 501(c)(3) organisations deductible by donors?
notes.back: Yes, as charitable contributions, except contributions to organisations testing for public safety.
notes.explanation: Testing for public safety is an exempt purpose, but Pub 557 carves it out of the deduction for donors.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Contributions to 501(c)(3) Organizations”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Contributions to domestic organizations described in this chapter, except organizations testing for public safety, are deductible as charitable contributions on the donor's federal income tax return.

notes.front: A donor gives $1,000 to a domestic 501(c)(3) food bank and $1,000 to a domestic 501(c)(3) organisation that tests products for public safety. Which gift is deductible as a charitable contribution?
notes.back: Only the $1,000 to the food bank; gifts to organisations testing for public safety are excepted.
notes.choices:
A) Only the food bank gift
B) Both gifts
C) Neither gift
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 557 excepts organisations testing for public safety from the deduction. C: the food bank gift is a deductible charitable contribution.
notes.explanation: Both organisations can be exempt, but Pub 557 carves testing for public safety out of the donor’s deduction.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Contributions to 501(c)(3) Organizations”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Contributions to domestic organizations described in this chapter, except organizations testing for public safety, are deductible as charitable contributions on the donor's federal income tax return.

notes.front: To qualify under section 501(c)(3), no part of the organisation’s net earnings may {{c1::inure to the benefit of private shareholders or individuals}}.
notes.back: Inure to the benefit of private shareholders or individuals.
notes.explanation: The organisation must show it will not be run for private interests such as its creator, the creator’s family or shareholders.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Section 501(c)(3) Organizations: requirements”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: No part of the organization's net earnings will inure to the benefit of private shareholders or individuals. You must establish that your organization won't be organized or operated for the benefit of private interests, such as the creator or the creator's family, shareholders of the organization

notes.front: A charity founder has the charity’s surplus paid each year to her own family as “bonuses” unrelated to any work. What is the exemption risk?
notes.back: Private inurement: net earnings are going to the creator’s family, which a 501(c)(3) organisation must not allow.
notes.choices:
A) Private inurement endangers exemption
B) None, if the charity’s programmes continue
C) None, because bonuses are wages
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule forbids any part of net earnings inuring to private individuals. C: labelling payments as bonuses does not stop them being private benefit to the creator’s family.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 names the creator and the creator’s family as private interests the organisation must not be run for.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Section 501(c)(3) Organizations: requirements”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: You must establish that your organization won't be organized or operated for the benefit of private interests, such as the creator or the creator's family, shareholders of the organization, other designated individuals

notes.front: A 501(c)(3) charity’s board wants to endorse a candidate for mayor in its newsletter, just once. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No: a 501(c)(3) organisation may not participate to any extent in a political campaign for or against a candidate.
notes.choices:
A) No, not to any extent
B) Yes, if it is an insubstantial part of activities
C) Yes, if it elects under section 501(h)
notes.choicesExplained: B: the insubstantial test applies to lobbying, not campaigns. C: section 501(h) concerns lobbying expenditures only.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 contrasts lobbying, which is limited to less than a substantial part, with campaign activity, which is barred to any extent.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Section 501(c)(3) Organizations: requirements”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: The organization won't, as a substantial part of its activities, attempt to influence legislation (unless it elects to come under the provisions allowing certain lobbying expenditures) or participate to any extent in a political campaign for or against any candidate for public office.

notes.front: What tax may a manager of a 501(c)(3) organisation owe for lobbying expenditures that disqualify it?
notes.back: A 5% tax on those lobbying expenditures, if the manager agreed knowing they were likely to cause disqualification.
notes.explanation: The tax turns on the manager’s knowledge: agreeing to the spending knowing disqualification was likely.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Tax on managers”, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: Managers may also be liable for a 5% tax on the lobbying expenditures that result in the disqualification of the organization. For the tax to apply, a manager would have to agree to the expenditures knowing that the expenditures were likely to result in the organization's not being described in section 501(c) (3).

notes.front: What generally separates a public charity from a private foundation?
notes.back: Public charities fall in excluded categories: generally broad public support, or supporting such organisations. The rest are private foundations.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 says the definition in effect splits 501(c)(3) organisations into these two classes.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Private Foundations”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: In effect, the definition divides these organizations into two classes, namely private foundations and public charities. Public charities are discussed later. Organizations that fall into the excluded categories are generally those that either have broad public support or actively function in a supporting relationship to those organizations.

notes.front: A newly formed 501(c)(3) organisation plans to fund its work through many small donations from the public. How can it avoid being classified as a private foundation from the start?
notes.back: Show, when it applies for exemption, that it can reasonably be expected to be publicly supported.
notes.choices:
A) Show it can reasonably be expected to be publicly supported
B) Wait five years and then apply
C) Nothing: every new 501(c)(3) is a private foundation
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 557 lets a new organisation be classified as publicly supported when it applies. C: the default can be displaced by that showing.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 says a new organisation is classified as publicly supported, not a private foundation, if it makes this showing when applying.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Public charity status”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: A new section 501(c) (3) organization will be classified as a publicly supported organization and not a private foundation if it can show when it applies for tax-exempt status that it reasonably can be expected to be publicly supported.

notes.front: The excise tax on the net investment income of private foundations is {{c1::1.39%}}.
notes.explanation: The 2019 legislation replaced the former 2% rate and its 1% special rate with this single rate.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Reminders: Tax on investment income of private foundations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: reduced the 2% excise tax on investment income of private foundations to 1.39%. At the same time, the legislation repealed the 1% special rate

notes.front: How must Form 1023, the application for recognition of 501(c)(3) exemption, be filed?
notes.back: Electronically, on Pay.gov.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 says Form 1023 and Form 1023-EZ must both be filed electronically.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Chapter 3”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Form 1023 and Form 1023-EZ must be filed electronically on Pay.gov.

notes.front: Which of these need not file Form 1023 to be exempt: a church, a local club (not a private foundation) with gross receipts normally under $5,000, or a new hospital?
notes.back: The church and the small club need not file Form 1023; the new hospital must apply.
notes.choices:
A) The church and the small club
B) All three
C) Only the church
notes.choicesExplained: B: a hospital is not in either excepted group. C: organisations (other than private foundations) normally under $5,000 of gross receipts are also excepted.
notes.explanation: Pub 557 lists churches and organisations (other than private foundations) normally having gross receipts of not more than $5,000 among those that need not apply.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Organizations not required to file Form 1023”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: conventions or associations of churches, or integrated auxiliaries of a church, such as a men's or women's organization, religious school, mission society, or youth group. • Any organization (other than a private foundation) normally having annual gross receipts of not more than $5,000

notes.front: Exemption is usually effective from formation if the application is submitted within {{c1::27 months}} from the end of the month in which the organisation was organised.
notes.back: 27 months.
notes.explanation: An application inside this window lets recognition reach back to the date of formation; the clock starts at the month end.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Effective Date of Exemption”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: A determination letter recognizing exemption is usually effective as of the date of formation of an organization if, the organization submitted the application for recognition of exemption within 27 months from the end of the month in which it was organized

notes.front: A charity was organised on 12 February 2024. By what date must it submit Form 1023 for its exemption to reach back to formation, without relief?
notes.back: By 31 May 2026: 27 months from 29 February 2024, the end of the month of organisation.
notes.choices:
A) 31 May 2026
B) 12 May 2026
C) 12 February 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B: the 27 months run from the end of the month, not the day, of organisation. C: that is only 12 months.
notes.explanation: Step 1: the month of organisation ends 29 February 2024. Step 2: 27 months later is 31 May 2026.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Effective Date of Exemption”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: within 27 months from the end of the month in which it was organized

notes.front: A new 501(c)(3) organisation expects annual gross receipts of $40,000 and has assets of $300,000. Can it use Form 1023-EZ?
notes.back: No: Form 1023-EZ needs assets of $250,000 or less as well as gross receipts of $50,000 or less.
notes.choices:
A) No, its assets are too high
B) Yes, its receipts are under $50,000
C) Yes, any new organisation may
notes.choicesExplained: B: both limits must be met, and $300,000 of assets exceeds $250,000. C: the form is only for smaller organisations.
notes.explanation: Step 1: receipts $40,000 ≤ $50,000 passes. Step 2: assets $300,000 > $250,000 fails, so it files Form 1023.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Form 1023-EZ”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: You may be eligible to file Form 1023-EZ if you are a smaller organization (assets of $250,000 or less and annual gross receipts of $50,000 or less) seeking recognition of exemption under section 501(c)(3).

notes.front: Which form do organisations seeking exemption under section 501(a) other than as 501(c)(3), or under section 521, use, and how is it filed?
notes.back: Form 1024, submitted electronically on Pay.gov.
notes.explanation: As its title says, Form 1024 is the application for exemption under section 501(a) or section 521.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Reminders: Electronic Form 1024”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Form 1024, Application for Recognition of Exemption Under Section 501(a) or Section 521, must be submitted for electronic filing on Pay.gov.

notes.front: An exempt organisation must file Form 990 if it has gross receipts of {{c1::$200,000}} or more, or total assets of $500,000 or more at year end.
notes.explanation: Either test alone is enough to require Form 990.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “A. Who Must File”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Form 990 must be filed by an organization exempt from income tax under section 501(a) (including an organization that hasn't applied for recognition of exemption) if it has either (1) gross receipts greater than or equal to $200,000, or (2) total assets greater

notes.front: When may an exempt organisation file Form 990-EZ instead of Form 990?
notes.back: When gross receipts are less than $200,000 and year-end total assets are less than $500,000.
notes.explanation: Both figures must be under their limits; failing either one requires the full Form 990.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “Form 990-EZ”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If an organization has gross receipts less than $200,000 and total assets at the end of the tax year less than $500,000, it can choose to file Form 990-EZ

notes.front: An organisation that normally has gross receipts of {{c1::$50,000 or less}} must submit Form 990-N if it chooses not to file Form 990 or 990-EZ.
notes.back: $50,000 or less.
notes.explanation: It is the fallback for small organisations that do not file either of the longer returns.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “Form 990-N”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If an organization normally has gross receipts of $50,000 or less, it must submit Form 990-N, if it chooses not to file Form 990 or 990-EZ

notes.front: Which annual return does a private foundation file?
notes.back: Form 990-PF, not Form 990 or 990-EZ.
notes.explanation: The Form 990 instructions list private foundations among organisations that file Form 990-PF instead.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “B. Organizations Not Required To File Form 990 or 990-EZ”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: A private foundation (including a private operating foundation) exempt under section 501(c)(3) and described in section 509(a). Use Form 990-PF

notes.front: A public charity has gross receipts of $150,000 and total assets of $620,000 at year end. Which annual return must it file?
notes.back: Form 990: its assets are $500,000 or more, even though receipts are under $200,000.
notes.choices:
A) Form 990
B) Form 990-EZ
C) Form 990-N
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 990-EZ needs assets under $500,000 as well. C: Form 990-N is for gross receipts normally $50,000 or less.
notes.explanation: Step 1: receipts $150,000 < $200,000. Step 2: assets $620,000 ≥ $500,000, so the Form 990 test is met.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “A. Who Must File”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: if it has either (1) gross receipts greater than or equal to $200,000, or (2) total assets greater

notes.front: A small community society normally has gross receipts of $35,000 and chooses not to file Form 990 or 990-EZ. What must it submit?
notes.back: Form 990-N, the annual electronic notice.
notes.choices:
A) Form 990-N
B) Nothing
C) Form 990-PF
notes.choicesExplained: B: an organisation that does not file Form 990 or 990-EZ must still submit Form 990-N. C: Form 990-PF is for private foundations.
notes.explanation: $35,000 is within the $50,000-or-less limit, so Form 990-N is required if it skips the longer returns.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “Form 990-N”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If an organization normally has gross receipts of $50,000 or less, it must submit Form 990-N, if it chooses not to file Form 990 or 990-EZ

notes.front: An exempt organisation’s accounting year ends on 30 June 2025. By when is its Form 990 due (before any extension)?
notes.back: 17 November 2025: the 15th day of the 5th month is 15 November, a Saturday, so the next business day.
notes.choices:
A) 17 November 2025
B) 15 October 2025
C) 15 May 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the 4th month, the Form 1041 rule. C: 15 May is the date for a calendar-year filer.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 5 months after June is November. Step 2: 15 November 2025 is a Saturday, so the return is due Monday 17 November.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: File Form 990 by the 15th day of the 5th month after the organization's accounting period ends (May 15th for a calendar-year filer). If the due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, file on the next business day.

notes.front: An organisation with gross receipts of $180,000 files its Form 990 20 days late without reasonable cause. What is the failure-to-file penalty?
notes.back: $500: $25 a day × 20 days, below the cap of the lesser of $13,000 or 5% of gross receipts ($9,000).
notes.choicesExplained: B: $130 a day applies only above $1,309,500 of gross receipts. C: $9,000 is the cap, not the penalty.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $25 × 20 = $500. Step 2: cap = lesser of $13,000 or 5% × $180,000 = $9,000. Step 3: $500 is under the cap.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “H. Failure-To-File Penalties”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: a penalty of $25 a day, not to exceed the lesser of $13,000 or 5% of the gross receipts of the organization for the year, can be charged when a return is filed late

notes.front: An organisation that fails to file its annual return or notice for {{c1::3 consecutive years}} automatically loses its tax-exempt status.
notes.back: 3 consecutive years.
notes.explanation: Revocation takes effect on and after the due date of the third return or notice that was not filed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “Annual return requirement”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: If an organization fails to file an annual return or submit a notice as required for 3 consecutive years, its tax-exempt status is automatically revoked on and after the due date for filing its third annual return or notice.

notes.front: A calendar-year club with gross receipts of $20,000 submitted nothing for 2022, 2023 or 2024. What has happened to its exemption?
notes.back: It was automatically revoked from the due date of its 2024 return or notice, the third missed filing.
notes.choices:
A) Automatically revoked
B) Nothing, because it is too small to file
C) It will be revoked only after the Internal Revenue Service audits it
notes.choicesExplained: B: small organisations must still submit Form 990-N. C: revocation is automatic, not by audit.
notes.explanation: Three consecutive years unfiled trigger automatic revocation on the third due date.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990 (2025), “Annual return requirement”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: its tax-exempt status is automatically revoked on and after the due date for filing its third annual return or notice.

notes.front: Under the Taxpayer First Act of 2019, when must the Internal Revenue Service notify an organisation that it risks automatic revocation?
notes.back: After it has failed to file for 2 consecutive years.
notes.explanation: The notice is a warning after two missed years; automatic revocation follows a third.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Reminders: Automatic revocation”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Regarding automatic revocation for the failure to file a return or notice for 3 consecutive years, as required by section 6033, the Taxpayer First Act of 2019, P.L. 116-25, added a requirement that the IRS notify the organization after the organization has failed to file for 2 consecutive years.

notes.front: For unrelated business income, what makes an activity a trade or business?
notes.back: An activity carried on to produce income from selling goods or performing services, with intent to make a profit.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 makes profit intent essential to a trade or business.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Trade or business”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The term "trade or business" generally includes any activity conducted for the production of income from selling goods or performing services. An activity must be conducted with intent to make a profit to constitute a trade or business.

notes.front: When is an exempt organisation’s business activity regularly conducted?
notes.back: Ordinarily when it shows frequency and continuity and is pursued like comparable commercial activities of nonexempt organisations.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 compares the activity with how a commercial business would pursue it.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Regularly conducted”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Business activities of an exempt organization ordinarily are considered regularly conducted if they show a frequency and continuity, and are pursued in a manner similar to comparable commercial activities of nonexempt organizations.

notes.front: A conservation charity hires out its hall for weddings most weekends all year. A choir sells raffle tickets at one festival weekend a year. Which activity is regularly conducted?
notes.back: The year-round hall hire: it shows frequency and continuity like a commercial venue; a single festival weekend does not.
notes.choices:
A) The hall hire
B) The raffle stall
C) Both
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: one weekend a year lacks the frequency and continuity of comparable commercial activity.
notes.explanation: Regular conduct means frequency and continuity pursued like comparable commercial businesses, which a year-round weekly operation shows.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Regularly conducted”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Business activities of an exempt organization ordinarily are considered regularly conducted if they show a frequency and continuity, and are pursued in a manner similar to comparable commercial activities of nonexempt organizations.

notes.front: A charity runs a commercial dry-cleaning shop open to the public and spends all the profit on its homeless shelter. Is the shop substantially related to its exempt purpose?
notes.back: No: using the profits for the exempt purpose does not, alone, make the activity substantially related.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because the profits fund the shelter
C) Yes, because charities cannot have unrelated income
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 598 says use of the profits alone does not make the activity related. C: charities can and do have unrelated business income.
notes.explanation: Relatedness depends on the activity itself contributing to the exempt purpose, not on where the money goes.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Chapter 3. Unrelated Trade or Business”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Use by the organization, of the profits derived from this activity, does not, alone, make the activity substantially related to the performance by the organization of its exempt purpose or function.

notes.front: Is selling products that result from an exempt function an unrelated trade or business?
notes.back: Ordinarily not, if the product is sold in substantially the same state it is in when the exempt function is completed.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 uses the sale of articles made by people in rehabilitation training as its illustration.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Selling of products of exempt functions”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Ordinarily, selling products that result from the performance of exempt functions isn't an unrelated trade or business if the product is sold in substantially the same state it is in when the exempt functions are completed.

notes.front: A charity’s café is open to the public daily, but unpaid volunteers do substantially all the work. Is it an unrelated trade or business?
notes.back: No: a business in which substantially all the work is done without compensation is excluded.
notes.choices:
A) No, the volunteer exclusion applies
B) Yes, because it is open daily
C) Yes, unless the café sells donated food
notes.choicesExplained: B: regularity does not matter once the volunteer exclusion applies. C: the volunteer exclusion stands on its own.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 excludes any trade or business in which substantially all the work is performed without compensation.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Volunteer workforce”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Any trade or business in which substantially all the work is performed for the organization without compensation isn't an unrelated trade or business.

notes.front: A 501(c)(3) hospital runs a cafeteria, staffed by paid workers, primarily for its patients and employees. Is it an unrelated trade or business?
notes.back: No: a business a 501(c)(3) organisation carries on primarily for the convenience of its patients or employees is excluded.
notes.choices:
A) No, the convenience exclusion applies
B) Yes, because workers are paid
C) Yes, because catering is not medical care
notes.choicesExplained: B: paid staff matter for the volunteer exclusion, not this one. C: the convenience exclusion applies even though catering is not itself the exempt purpose.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 excludes businesses run primarily for the convenience of members, students, patients, officers or employees.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Convenience of members”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: A trade or business conducted by a 501(c)(3) organization or by a state college or university primarily for the convenience of its members, students, patients, officers, or employees isn't an unrelated trade or business.

notes.front: A hospice runs a year-round online auction, with paid staff, of artworks substantially all of which were donated to it. Is the auction an unrelated trade or business?
notes.back: No: selling merchandise substantially all of which was received as gifts or contributions is excluded.
notes.choices:
A) No, the donated-goods exclusion applies
B) Yes, because it uses paid staff
C) Yes, because it competes with commercial shops
notes.choicesExplained: B: paid staff defeat only the volunteer exclusion. C: competition does not matter once this exclusion applies.
notes.explanation: Pub 598 excludes selling merchandise that the organisation received substantially all as gifts or contributions.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Selling donated merchandise”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: A trade or business that consists of selling merchandise, substantially all of which the organization received as gifts or contributions, isn't an unrelated trade or business.

notes.front: An exempt organisation must file Form 990-T if it has gross income of {{c1::$1,000}} or more from a regularly conducted unrelated trade or business.
notes.explanation: Gross income here means gross receipts minus the cost of goods sold.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990-T (2025), “Who Must File”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: $1,000 or more from a regularly conducted unrelated trade or business (see Regulations section 1.6012-2(e)). Gross income is gross receipts minus the cost of goods sold

notes.front: A charity’s gift shop sells unrelated goods regularly: gross receipts $3,400, cost of goods sold $2,600. Must it file Form 990-T?
notes.back: No: gross income is $3,400 − $2,600 = $800, below the $1,000 filing threshold.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because gross receipts exceed $1,000
C) Yes, whenever there is any unrelated income
notes.choicesExplained: B: the threshold uses gross income (receipts less cost of goods sold), not gross receipts. C: the threshold is $1,000 of gross income.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $3,400 − $2,600 = $800 of gross income. Step 2: $800 < $1,000, so no Form 990-T is required on this basis.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990-T (2025), “Who Must File”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Gross income is gross receipts minus the cost of goods sold

notes.front: An exempt organisation’s only unrelated business has gross income of $30,000 and directly connected deductions of $12,000, with no net operating loss. What is its UBTI?
notes.choicesExplained: B: leaves out the $1,000 specific deduction. C: leaves out the $12,000 of directly connected deductions.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $30,000 − $12,000 = $18,000. Step 2: less the $1,000 specific deduction = $17,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990-T (2025), “Line 8. Specific Deduction”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: A specific deduction of $1,000 is allowed except for computing the NOL and the net operating loss deduction under section 172.

notes.front: By when must most exempt organisations file Form 990-T, and which filers use an earlier date?
notes.back: Most: 15th day of the 5th month after year end. A Roth IRA, Coverdell ESA and similar accounts: 15th day of the 4th month.
notes.explanation: The earlier date applies only to the retirement and savings accounts the instructions name.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 990-T (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: a Roth IRA, a Coverdell ESA, or an Archer MSA must file Form 990-T by the 15th day of the 4th month after the end of its tax year. All other organizations must file Form 990-T by the 15th day of the 5th month after the end of their tax years.

notes.front: What is debt-financed property for UBTI purposes?
notes.back: Property held to produce income with acquisition indebtedness at any time in the tax year (or the 12 months before disposal).
notes.explanation: Income from such property is included in UBTI in proportion to the debt on the property.
notes.source: Publication 598 (Rev. March 2021), Tax on Unrelated Business Income of Exempt Organizations, “Debt-Financed Property”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: The amount of income included is proportionate to the debt on the property. Debt-Financed Property In general, the term "debt-financed property" means any property held to produce income (including gain from its disposition) for which there is an acquisition indebtedness at any time during the tax year
